definition: Too great, deep, or intense to be described in words.
example: The faded photograph stirred an ineffable longing for a house he had never actually seen.
nuance: Ineffable usually praises something wondrous or profound, while unspeakable more often suggests something too awful to name.
prompt: A young violinist tries to describe the moment she first heard a full orchestra play.
options: She said the opening chord filled her with an ineffable joy she still cannot explain.
Her ineffable bow strokes failed to produce any sound at all.
She described the ineffable sound fully with a short, precise list of adjectives.
The ineffable squeak of the rehearsal room door annoyed every musician in the string section.
reasons: A feeling so deep that she cannot put it into words fits the word exactly.
This confuses the word with ineffectual; it is about what can't be expressed, not what doesn't work.
If a few adjectives capture it completely, the sound was easy to express, not beyond words.
A squeaky door is a minor, easily named nuisance, not an overwhelming experience.

practice.prompt: A hiker reaches a quiet mountain lake just as the sun rises.
options: The hiker felt an ineffable stillness as mist lifted off the silver water.
The ineffable error on her trail map was cleared up once she checked its printing date.
The hiker summed up the ineffable view in three plain words: nice, blue, cold.
Her ineffable blister made the last mile of the trail slow and painful.
reasons: A calm so profound that language falls short is exactly what the word conveys.
A puzzle that gets explained is inexplicable at most; the word concerns experiences beyond words.
A view captured by three ordinary words was easy to put into language.
A blister is an ordinary, easily described discomfort, not something transcending language.
